translations.idiomatic: Still, statute must stay balanced—never overshoot.

sentences.zh: 臣以為女人有三從之義，無自專之道，出適他族，還喪父母，降其服紀，所以明外成之節，異在室之恩。

translations.literal: Your servant believes women observe three obediences and lack independent agency; married into another surname and returning to mourn parents they lower mourning grades—thereby marking outsider ritual boundaries distinct from daughters still unmarried.
translations.idiomatic: Women follow father, husband, son—rites distinguish maidens from wives.

sentences.zh: 而父母有罪，追刑已出之女；

translations.literal: Yet when parents sin, punishment pursues daughters already married away;
translations.idiomatic: Parents’ guilt nevertheless dragged married daughters back under the blade.

sentences.zh: 夫黨見誅，又有隨姓之戮。

translations.literal: When husband’s faction is executed they again suffer surname-linked slaughter.
translations.idiomatic: If husbands’ clans fell, wives died twice over.

sentences.zh: 一人之身，內外受辟。

translations.literal: One body suffers executions from both inner and outer kin.
translations.idiomatic: A single woman answered both natal and marital guilt.

sentences.zh: 今女既嫁，則為異姓之妻；

translations.literal: Once wed she belongs to another surname’s wife;
translations.idiomatic: Marriage transfers loyalty to the husband’s house.

sentences.zh: 如或產育，則為他族之母，此為元惡之所忽。

translations.literal: If she bears sons she becomes mother to another lineage—points vicious regimes overlook.
translations.idiomatic: Motherhood anchors her with her children’s clan—tyrants ignored this.

sentences.zh: 戮無辜之所重，於防則不足懲奸亂之源，於情則傷孝子之心。

translations.literal: Slaughtering innocents weighs heavily: deterrence cannot plug treason’s spring yet sentiment wounds filial sons.
translations.idiomatic: Executing guiltless women neither stops rebellion nor consoles loyal sons.

sentences.zh: 男不得罪於他族，而女獨嬰戮於二門，非所以哀矜女弱，蠲明法制之本分也。

translations.literal: Men incur no guilt from alien clans yet women alone endure blades from two gates—not how to pity frail wives or clarify law’s core divisions.
translations.idiomatic: Men escaped cross-clan guilt while women died twice—hardly mercy or clarity.

sentences.zh: 臣以為在室之女，從父母之誅；

translations.literal: Your servant proposes daughters still at home follow parental sentences;
translations.idiomatic: Unmarried daughters share parental punishment.

sentences.zh: 既醮之婦，從夫家之罰。

translations.literal: Women who have drunk nuptial wine follow husband-house penalties.
translations.idiomatic: Wives answer husband-house crimes alone.

sentences.zh: 宜改舊科，以為永制。

translations.literal: Old statutes should change into perpetual precedent.
translations.idiomatic: Codify this split forever.

sentences.zh: 」於是有詔改定律令。

translations.literal: Thereupon an edict revised statutes and commands.
translations.idiomatic: An imperial order rewrote the law accordingly.

sentences.zh: 文帝為晉王，患前代律令本注煩雜，陳群、劉邵雖經改革，而科網本密，又叔孫、郭、馬、杜諸儒章句，但取鄭氏，又為偏黨，未可承用。

translations.literal: While Crown Prince Wen governed he saw earlier statutes and glosses as tangled; though Chen Qun and Liu Shao had streamlined them, the statutory mesh stayed dense, and the houses of Shusun, Guo, Ma, and Du—yet canonizing only Zheng Xuan—skewed partisan and could not serve wholesale.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Zhao complained that Wei codes stayed bloated and Zheng-only commentary biased.

sentences.zh: 於是令賈充定法律，令與太傅鄭沖、司徒荀顗、中書監荀勖、中軍將軍羊祜、中護軍王業、廷尉杜友、守河南尹杜預、散騎侍郎裴楷、潁川太守周雄、齊相郭頎、騎都尉成公綏、尚書郎柳軌及吏部令史榮邵等十四人典其事，就漢九章增十一篇，仍其族類，正其體號，改舊律為《刑名》、《法例》，辨《囚律》為《告劾》、《系訊》、《斷獄》，分《盜律》為《請賕》、《詐偽》、《水火》、《毀亡》，因事類為《衛宮》、《違制》，撰《周官》為《諸侯律》，合二十篇，六百二十條，二萬七千六百五十七言。

translations.literal: Thereupon he ordered Jia Chong to settle statutes, together with Grand Tutor Zheng Chong, Minister Xun Yi, Palace Secretariat Director Xun Xu, Central Army General Yang Hu, Central Protector Wang Ye, Commandant of Justice Du You, acting Henan Intendant Du Yu, Cavalry Gentleman Pei Kai, Yingchuan prefect Zhou Xiong, Qi chancellor Guo Qi, Commandant of Cavalry Cheng Gongshui, Palace Gentleman Liu Gui, and clerks Rong Shao—fourteen officers overseeing the project—building on Han’s nine chapters with eleven new fascicles, preserving taxonomies and correcting titles, retitling old statutes as Punishment Names and Legal Precedents, splitting Prison law into Accusation, Detention, and Trial, dividing Robber law into Soliciting Bribes, Fraud, Fire and Water, and Destruction, grouping situational matters as Palace Guard and Violating Regulations, adapting the Rites of Zhou into Feudal Lords law—twenty fascicles, 620 articles, 27,657 characters.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Zhao tasked Jia Chong, Zheng Chong, the Xun cousins, Yang Hu, Du Yu, Pei Kai, and ten others to reshape Wei law into twenty Jin fascicles—620 clauses built from Han’s nine chapters plus reorganized robbery, fraud, palace, and feudal sections totaling nearly twenty-eight thousand characters.

sentences.zh: 蠲其苛穢，存其清約，事從中典，歸於益時。

translations.literal: They cut filth and kept essentials—matters follow central canons and aim to benefit the age.
translations.idiomatic: Editors stripped cruft, kept crisp rules, and tuned everything to contemporary needs.

sentences.zh: 其餘未宜除者，若軍事、田農、酤酒，未得皆從人心，權設其法，太平當除，故不入律，悉以為令。

translations.literal: Matters not yet fit for repeal—such as military affairs, farming, or liquor monopolies—could not all follow popular wishes; they provisionally set laws to be repealed in Great Peace, therefore not embedded in statutes but collected as edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Military, agrarian, and liquor rules stayed provisional edicts until a future peaceful reign could prune them.

sentences.zh: 施行制度，以此設教，違令有罪則入律。

translations.literal: Institutions implementing policy used these for instruction—violating edicts became statutory crime.
translations.idiomatic: Administrative handbooks taught policy; breaching those edicts triggered codified penalties.

sentences.zh: 其常事品式章程，各還其府，為故事。

translations.literal: Routine administrative forms and memorial templates returned to their bureaus as precedent dossiers.
translations.idiomatic: Everyday paperwork stayed departmental precedent rather than criminal code.

sentences.zh: 減梟斬族誅從坐之條，除謀反適養母出女嫁皆不復還坐父母棄市，省禁固相告之條，去捕亡、亡沒為官奴婢之制。

translations.literal: They reduced provisions on displaying heads, waist-cutting, clan execution, and accessory sitting; removed returning parents to marketplace execution for treason, adopted heirs, divorced daughters; dropped mutual denunciation imprisonment; abolished arrest fugitive statutes and enslavement of fugitives’ kin.
translations.idiomatic: Penal reform softened exposure executions, limited clan guilt for treason and adoption cases, scrapped denunciation prisons, and ended fugitive enslavement rules.

sentences.zh: 輕過誤老少女人當罰金杖罰者，皆令半之。

translations.literal: Light offenses, mistakes, old age, youth, or women liable for cash or cane had sentences halved.
translations.idiomatic: Fines and beatings for minors, seniors, women, and petty slips were automatically cut in half.

sentences.zh: 重奸伯叔母之令，棄市。

translations.literal: They strengthened the statute on violating paternal uncles and aunts—marketplace execution.
translations.idiomatic: Incest with uncles or aunts now meant immediate public execution.

sentences.zh: 淫寡女，三歲刑。

translations.literal: Fornicating with widows brought three years labor.
translations.idiomatic: Seducing bereaved women earned three years penal labor.

sentences.zh: 崇嫁娶之要，一以下娉為正，不理私約。

translations.literal: They elevated marriage essentials—only formal betrothal gifts counted; private pledges were ignored.
translations.idiomatic: Marriage validity rested solely on documented bride-price, not secret promises.

sentences.zh: 峻禮教之防，准五服以制罪也。

translations.literal: They fortified ritual barriers and matched punishments to the five mourning grades.
translations.idiomatic: Law enforced mourning hierarchies when calibrating criminal guilt.

sentences.zh: 凡律令合二千九百二十六條，十二萬六千三百言，六十卷，故事三十卷。

translations.literal: Statutes and edicts together numbered 2,926 articles, 126,300 characters, sixty scrolls; precedent dossiers thirty scrolls.
translations.idiomatic: The codex stacked 2,926 provisions across sixty volumes plus thirty precedent fascicles.

sentences.zh: 泰始三年，事畢，表上。

translations.literal: In Taishi third year the work finished and they memorialized it upward.
translations.idiomatic: Taishi 3 (267 CE) saw the finished code presented to the throne.

sentences.zh: 武帝詔曰：「昔蕭何以定律令受封，叔孫通制儀為奉常，賜金五百斤，弟子百人皆為郎。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu edicted: "Formerly Xiao He earned ennoblement for fixing statutes; Shusun Tong framed ceremonies as libationer with five hundred jin of gold and a hundred disciples made gentlemen.
translations.idiomatic: Wudi quoted Han precedents: Xiao He and Shusun Tong earned honors for codifying law and ritual.

sentences.zh: 夫立功立事，古今之所重，宜加祿賞，其詳考差敘。

translations.literal: Establishing merit has always mattered—add salaries and rewards; investigate ranks carefully.
translations.idiomatic: Reward the compilers commensurate with their service.

sentences.zh: 輒如詔簡異弟子百人，隨才品用，賞帛萬餘匹。

translations.literal: Accordingly the edict selected a hundred outstanding disciples, assigning posts by talent, and awarded more than ten thousand bolts of silk.
translations.idiomatic: A hundred junior scholars won appointments and ten thousand rolls of silk.

sentences.zh: 」武帝親自臨講，使裴楷執讀。

translations.literal: " Emperor Wu personally attended the lecture and had Pei Kai read aloud.
translations.idiomatic: Wudi presided while Pei Kai recited the new code.

sentences.zh: 四年正月，大赦天下，乃班新律。

translations.literal: Fourth year, first month, he proclaimed a general amnesty and promulgated the new statutes.
translations.idiomatic: In the first month of year four he amnestied the realm and published the Jin code.

sentences.zh: 其後，明法掾張裴又注律，表上之，其要曰：

translations.literal: Later legal clerk Zhang Pei annotated the statutes, memorialized them, summarizing:
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Pei’s statutory commentary begins:

sentences.zh: 律始於《刑名》者，所以定罪制也；

translations.literal: Statutes open with Punishment Names because that fascicle fixes guilt and measures.
translations.idiomatic: Punishment Names opens the code because it defines offense labels and scales.

sentences.zh: 終於《諸侯》者，所以畢其政也。

translations.literal: They end with Feudal Lords because that fascicle completes governance.
translations.idiomatic: Feudal Lords closes the book because it finishes jurisdictional rules.

sentences.zh: 王政布于上，諸侯奉于下，禮樂撫於中，故有三才之義焉，其相須而成，若一體焉。

translations.literal: Royal policy spreads above, feudal lords obey below, ritual and music soothe within—thus the triad of heaven, earth, and man mutually completes like one body.
translations.idiomatic: Editorial structure mirrors heaven-earth-man coordination across statutes.

sentences.zh: 《刑名》所以經略罪法之輕重，正加減之等差，明發眾篇之多義，補其章條之不足，較舉上下綱領。

translations.literal: Punch Names threads severity of offenses, corrects scales of increase and decrease, releases manifold meanings across chapters, repairs insufficient clauses, and aligns overarching frameworks.
translations.idiomatic: The opening fascicle harmonizes sentencing ladders across the entire code.

sentences.zh: 其犯盜賊、詐偽、請賕者，則求罪於此，作役、水火、畜養、守備之細事，皆求之作本名。

translations.literal: Robbery, fraud, and bribery seek guilt definitions here; corvée labor, fire and water, livestock, guard duties seek native fascicle titles.
translations.idiomatic: Core crimes resolve through Names while petty administrative offenses cite their titled chapters.

sentences.zh: 告訊為之心舌，捕系為之手足，斷獄為之定罪，名例齊其制。

translations.literal: Accusation and interrogation serve as tongue; arrest and binding as limbs; trial verdicts fix guilt—general principles knit the system.
translations.idiomatic: Litigation flows tongue-to-hand-to-verdict under unified principles.

sentences.zh: 自始及終，往而不窮，變動無常，周流四極，上下無方，不離於法律之中也。

translations.literal: From beginning to end movement never exhausts; changes lack fixity; it circles four extremes and rises or sinks without fixed direction—yet never departs from legal order.
translations.idiomatic: Flexible doctrine stays anchored despite exhaustive hypotheticals.

sentences.zh: 其知而犯之謂之故，意以為然謂之失，違忠欺上謂之謾，背信藏巧謂之詐，虧禮廢節謂之不敬，兩訟相趣謂之鬥，兩和相害謂之戲，無變斬擊謂之賊，不意誤犯謂之過失，逆節絕理謂之不道，陵上僭貴謂之惡逆，將害未發謂之戕，唱首先言謂之造意，二人對議謂之謀，制眾建計謂之率，不和謂之強，攻惡謂之略，三人謂之群，取非其物謂之盜，貨財之利謂之贓：凡二十者，律義之較名也。

translations.literal: Knowing yet offending is called intentional; believing it correct is called negligent fault; betraying loyalty and deceiving superiors is called deceit; breaking faith and hiding craft is called fraud; violating ritual propriety is called irreverence; two lawsuits rushing together is called affray; mutual consent harming is called horseplay; unchanged hacking blows are called banditry; unintentional mistake is called accidental fault; opposing cosmic order is called lack of the Way; bullying superiors and usurping honor is called monstrous rebellion; intending harm not yet launched is called plotted assault; first voicing a scheme is called initiating intent; two plotting together is called conspiracy; directing masses plotting is called leading; unwilling coercion is called forced assault; seizing evil opportunity is called raid; three conspirators is called gang; taking goods not one’s own is called theft; profiting goods is called embezzlement—in all twenty items defining comparative statutory labels.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Pei lists twenty definitional contrasts—intent versus negligence, fraud versus jest—that judges use like diagnostic labels.

sentences.zh: 夫律者，當慎其變，審其理。

translations.literal: Statutes must heed transformations and examine rationales.
translations.idiomatic: Good adjudication tracks shifting facts and moral nuance.

sentences.zh: 若不承用詔書，無故失之刑，當從贖。

translations.literal: When someone fails to apply edict letters without cause the negligence punishment ought to follow redemption.
translations.idiomatic: Ignorant mishandling of imperial orders qualifies for redeemable fines.

sentences.zh: 謀反之同伍，實不知情，當從刑。

translations.literal: Neighbors of rebels who truly knew nothing ought nonetheless face statutory punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Five-house rebel neighbors bear graded punishment even if ignorant—a deliberate severity.

sentences.zh: 此故失之變也。

translations.literal: These illustrate transformations between intentional and negligent fault.
translations.idiomatic: Such edge cases refine intent doctrine.

sentences.zh: 卑與尊鬥，皆為賊。

translations.literal: When inferior and superior fight both count as banditry.
translations.idiomatic: Any status mix in brawls triggers bandit-law scrutiny.

sentences.zh: 鬥之加兵刃水火中，不得為戲，戲之重也。

translations.literal: If fight introduces blades fire or water mid-struggle it cannot be horseplay—horseplay’s gravity differs.
translations.idiomatic: Introducing lethal tools upgrades jest to assault.

sentences.zh: 向人室廬道徑射，不得為過，失之禁也。

translations.literal: Shooting toward residences paths cannot count as accident—the prohibition covers inadvertence.
translations.idiomatic: Reckless shooting near dwellings breaks absolute bans regardless of intent.

sentences.zh: 都城人眾中走馬殺人，當為賊，賊之似也。

translations.literal: Galloping horses through crowded capital streets killing people counts as banditry—akin to predatory crime.
translations.idiomatic: Fatal stampedes in royal cities mimic malicious killing.

sentences.zh: 過失似賊，戲似鬥，鬥而殺傷傍人，又似誤，盜傷縛守似強盜，呵人取財似受賕，囚辭所連似告劾，諸勿聽理似故縱，持質似恐猲。

translations.literal: Accidental injury resembling banditry, horseplay resembling affray, affray injuring bystanders resembling mistake, thieves injuring bound guards resembling robbery, berating people for property resembling bribery, prisoner statements chaining others resembling accusation, ignoring hearings resembling connivance, hostage-taking resembling terror—all blur categories.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Pei catalogs mimetic offenses requiring careful discrimination.

sentences.zh: 如此之比，皆為無常之格也。

translations.literal: Patterns such as these constitute fluid comparative grids.
translations.idiomatic: Judges rely on these sliding scales when labels collide.

sentences.zh: 五刑不簡，正於五罰，五罰不服，正於五過，意善功惡，以金贖之。

translations.literal: When five punishments resist simplification rectify with five fines; when fines resist obey five excess judgments—good intent yet bad outcome redeems with metal.
translations.idiomatic: Classical five-fine ladder fills gaps when corporal punishment misfires.

sentences.zh: 故律制，生罪不過十四等，死刑不過三，徒加不過六，囚加不過五，累作不過十一歲，累笞不過千二百，刑等不過一歲，金等不過四兩。

translations.literal: Thus statutes cap living offenses at fourteen grades, capital at three, labor aggravation at six, imprisonment aggravation at five, cumulative labor not beyond eleven years, cumulative flogging not beyond 1,200 strokes, sentence increments within one year, cash increments within four taels.
translations.idiomatic: The code therefore caps gradations at every step: no more than fourteen living-crime ranks, three capital grades, six labor enhancements, five detention enhancements, eleven cumulative labor years, twelve hundred cumulative strokes, one-year sentence increments, and four-tael cash increments.

sentences.zh: 月贖不計日，日作不拘月，歲數不疑閏。

translations.literal: Monthly redemption ignores partial days; daily labor ignores calendar months; yearly counts ignore intercalary months.
translations.idiomatic: Sentence accounting ignores fractional moons or leap months.

sentences.zh: 不以加至死，並死不復加。

translations.literal: Aggravation never stacks to death; combined death cannot stack further.
translations.idiomatic: Capital punishment caps aggravation ladders.

sentences.zh: 不可累者，故有並數；

translations.literal: What cannot accumulate therefore uses parallel numbering;
translations.idiomatic: Some bans run concurrently rather than sequentially.

sentences.zh: 不可並數，乃累其加。

translations.literal: what cannot run parallel then stacks increments.
translations.idiomatic: Other offenses aggregate aggravation instead.

sentences.zh: 以加論者，但得其加；

translations.literal: When judging by aggravation capture only the aggravating increment;
translations.idiomatic: Aggravation sentencing isolates the marginal penalty.

sentences.zh: 與加同者，連得其本。

translations.literal: when identical with aggravation link back to base offense.
translations.idiomatic: Matching tiers revert to baseline guilt.

sentences.zh: 不在次者，不以通論。

translations.literal: When outside sequence do not blend doctrines.
translations.idiomatic: Off-sequence crimes resist unified analogy.

sentences.zh: 以人得罪與人同，以法得罪與法同。

translations.literal: Personal guilt aligns with persons; statutory guilt aligns with statutes.
translations.idiomatic: Personal versus procedural guilt follow distinct tracks.

sentences.zh: 侵生害死，不可齊其防；

translations.literal: Injuring the living versus harming the dead cannot share identical defenses;
translations.idiomatic: Harm to corpses versus persons demands different shields.

sentences.zh: 親疏公私，不可常其教。

translations.literal: Kinship distance and public versus private cannot fix one universal teaching.
translations.idiomatic: Public versus familial crimes need tailored instruction.

sentences.zh: 禮樂崇於上，故降其刑；

translations.literal: Because ritual and music are lofty above punishments lighten;
translations.idiomatic: Higher ritual standing earns lighter penalties.

sentences.zh: 刑法閑于下，故全其法。

translations.literal: because punishments operate below the statutes preserve completeness.
translations.idiomatic: Lower strata rely on exhaustive statute to preserve full protection.

sentences.zh: 是故尊卑敘，仁義明，九族親，王道平也。

translations.literal: Therefore noble and base order themselves; benevolence and righteousness clarify; nine kinship circles harmonize; kingly way levels.
translations.idiomatic: Balanced gradations yield humane clarity across kin networks.

sentences.zh: 律有事狀相似而罪名相涉者，若加威勢下手取財為強盜，不自知亡為縛守，將中有惡言為恐猲，不以罪名呵為呵人，以罪名呵為受賕，劫召其財為持質。

translations.literal: Statutes contain fact-patterns resembling each other yet implicating different crimes—using intimidation to seize property is robbery; unknowingly guarding escapees is custodial binding; threatening with wicked words is terror extortion; berating without naming crime is verbal seizure; berating with named crime is bribery; seizing property by coercion is hostage-taking.
translations.idiomatic: Six intimidation economies share coercion yet earn distinct labels—robbery, jailbreak assistance, terror, shakedown, bribery, hostage seizure.

sentences.zh: 此六者，以威勢得財而名殊者也。

translations.literal: These six gain wealth through awe though titles differ.
translations.idiomatic: Same coercive profit stream splits across six statutory names.

sentences.zh: 即不求自與為受求，所監求而後取為盜贓，輸入呵受為留難，斂人財物積藏於官為擅賦，加歐擊之為戮辱。

translations.literal: Not requesting yet accepting is soliciting bribes; supervisors demanding then taking is embezzled theft; funneling seized goods through authorities is obstruction; stockpiling levies inside offices is unauthorized taxation; superimposed beatings become humiliating injury.
translations.idiomatic: Solicitation, supervised theft, bureaucratic obstruction, and illegal surcharges each refine bribery’s shades.

sentences.zh: 諸如此類，皆為以威勢得財而罪相似者也。

translations.literal: All such cases share coercive enrichment with similar guilt.
translations.idiomatic: Wealth-by-intimidation cases remain cognate despite label shifts.

sentences.zh: 夫刑者，司理之官；

translations.literal: Punishment is the office of managing principle;
translations.idiomatic: Criminal law administers underlying pattern.

sentences.zh: 理者，求情之機，情者，心神之使。

translations.literal: Principle is the trigger for seeking facts; facts are the envoys of mind and spirit.
translations.idiomatic: Legal reasoning traces outward facts to inward intent.

sentences.zh: 心感則情動於中，而形於言？

translations.literal: When the mind stirs, emotion moves within and takes form in words?
translations.idiomatic: Does not emotion voice itself outward once the heart stirs?

sentences.zh: 暢于四支，發於事業。

translations.literal: It extends through the four limbs and emerges in affairs.
translations.idiomatic: It flows through the four limbs and finds expression in every deed.

sentences.zh: 是故奸人心愧而面赤，內怖而色奪。

translations.literal: Therefore wicked people inwardly shame yet flush red, inwardly fear yet lose color.
translations.idiomatic: Villains blanch or flush when truth closes in.

sentences.zh: 論罪者務本其心，審其情，精其事，近取諸身，遠取諸物，然後乃可以正刑。

translations.literal: Sentencers must root in mind, examine facts, refine incidents, take evidence from the body, seek analogies in things—only then can punishment be just.
translations.idiomatic: Judges must triangulate motive, fact, and physical tells before sentencing.

sentences.zh: 仰手似乞，俯手似奪，捧手似謝，擬手似訴，拱臂似自首，攘臂似格鬥，矜莊似威，怡悅似福，喜怒憂歡，貌在聲色。

translations.literal: Upturned hands resemble begging; downturned hands resemble seizing; cupped hands resemble thanks; imitative hands resemble pleading; folded arms resemble surrender; flung arms resemble brawl; composed bearing resembles awe; glad faces resemble blessing; joy, anger, grief, pleasure sit in voice and countenance.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Pei lists gesture and expression lexicons for inferring intent.

sentences.zh: 奸真猛弱，候在視息。

translations.literal: Cunning or honesty, violence or weakness—await breath and glance.
translations.idiomatic: Breathing tempo and eye flicker betray truth.

sentences.zh: 出口有言當為告，下手有禁當為賊，喜子殺怒子當為戲，怒子殺喜子當為賊。

translations.literal: Speech exiting constitutes accusation; forbidden blows descending constitute banditry; joyful son killing angry son counts as horseplay; angry son killing joyful son counts as banditry.
translations.idiomatic: Voice versus fist distinguishes accusation from assault; mood contrasts redefine jest versus malice.

sentences.zh: 諸如此類，自非至精不能極其理也。

translations.literal: Analogies such as these demand utmost refinement or principle stays obscure.
translations.idiomatic: Only meticulous inference clarifies such overlaps.

sentences.zh: 律之名例，非正文而分明也。

translations.literal: Statutory general principles are not main-text clauses yet remain luminous.
translations.idiomatic: General Part doctrines illuminate without occupying numbered articles.

sentences.zh: 若八十，非殺傷人，他皆勿論，即誣告謀反者反坐。

translations.literal: If age eighty, except for killing or wounding another, all else goes undiscussed; false accusers of plotting rebellion sit reversed.
translations.idiomatic: Octogenarians skip liability except for homicide, while false accusers of treason face reverse judgment.

sentences.zh: 十歲，不得告言人；

translations.literal: At age ten one may not accuse others in court.
translations.idiomatic: Children under ten cannot file suit.

sentences.zh: 即奴婢捍主，主得謁殺之。

translations.literal: If bond servants strike masters, the master may report and execute them.
translations.idiomatic: When slaves resist masters, the master may petition to kill them.

sentences.zh: 賊燔人廬舍積聚，盜贓五匹以上，棄市；

translations.literal: Bandits who burn houses or storehouses, or steal five bolts of goods or more, face marketplace execution.
translations.idiomatic: Arson and major theft above five bolts drew public execution.

sentences.zh: 即燔官府積聚盜，亦當與同。

translations.literal: If burning official storehouses or stealing there, treat the same.
translations.idiomatic: Official granaries burned or robbed faced identical sanctions.

sentences.zh: 歐人教令者與同罪，即令人歐其父母，不可與行者同得重也。

translations.literal: Those who instruct beatings share the striker's guilt; ordering someone to beat parents cannot receive the same heavy sentence as the striker.
translations.idiomatic: Instigating assault tracks accomplice liability; ordering parental assault differs from acting.

sentences.zh: 若得遺物強取強乞之類，無還贓法隨例畀之文。

translations.literal: If forcibly taking lost property or begging by force—when no restitution statute exists—follow exemplar rules on surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Forced recovery of lost goods uses precedent restitution clauses.

sentences.zh: 法律中諸不敬，違儀失式，及犯罪為公為私，贓入身不入身，皆隨事輕重取法，以例求其名也。

translations.literal: Within statutes every category of irreverence, ritual lapse, public versus private crime, embezzlement entering person or coffers—each follows incident severity to retrieve the proper label.
translations.idiomatic: Statutory taxonomy sorts ritual faults, public/private guilt, and tangible versus intangible spoils by degrees.

sentences.zh: 夫理者，精玄之妙，不可以一方行也；

translations.literal: Principle is subtle mystery—it cannot travel on one track.
translations.idiomatic: Legal principle refuses single-track formulas.

sentences.zh: 律者，幽理之奧，不可以一體守也。

translations.literal: Statute is abstruse principle—it cannot be guarded as one rigid body.
translations.idiomatic: Written law cannot freeze into one rigid mold.

sentences.zh: 或計過以配罪，或化略以循常，或隨事以盡情，或趣舍以從時，或推重以立防，或引輕而就下。

translations.literal: Sometimes match fault to crime, sometimes simplify outline to follow norms, sometimes exhaust sentiment with facts, sometimes advance or retreat with seasons, sometimes erect heavy fences, sometimes draw light toward leniency.
translations.idiomatic: Judges weigh fault-matching, simplified defaults, fact-sensitive mercy, seasonal policy shifts, harsh deterrence, or lenient relief.

sentences.zh: 公私廢避之宜，除削重輕之變，皆所以臨時觀釁，使用法執詮者幽於未制之中，采其根牙之微，致之於機格之上，稱輕重於豪銖，考輩類于參伍，然後乃可以理直刑正。

translations.literal: Matters of avoiding public or private duty, cutting or amplifying severity—all rely on watching cracks in the moment so jurists holding glossaries probe unreached scenarios, capture root tendrils, raise them to procedural frameworks, balance weight on fine scales, compare kinds in five-fold arrays—only then can principle straighten and punishments align.
translations.idiomatic: Elastic doctrines let judges weigh mitigations, scan microscopic facts, and align sentences through layered analogy.

sentences.zh: 夫奉聖典者若操刀執繩，刀妄加則傷物，繩妄彈則侵直。

translations.literal: Those wielding sacred canons are like holding knife or cord—misapplied knife wounds creatures, mis-snapped cord wrongs the straight.
translations.idiomatic: Judges wield law like blade and plumb-line—careless use mis-harms.

sentences.zh: 梟首者惡之長，斬刑者罪之大，棄市者死之下，髡作者刑之威，贖罰者誤之誡。

translations.literal: Displaying heads crowns villainy; waist-cutting marks greatest guilt; marketplace execution ranks lowest death; shaved labor shows penal awe; redemption warns negligence.
translations.idiomatic: Five punishments grade horror from head-display to fines.

sentences.zh: 王者立此五刑，所以寶君子而逼小人，故為敕慎之經，皆擬《周易》有變通之體焉。

translations.literal: The king institutes these five punishments to treasure gentlemen and press petty men—therefore canonical caution threads through them, each patterned on Zhou Changes' adaptive mode.
translations.idiomatic: Royal punishments elevate virtue while intimidating vice, modeled on Change's flexibility.

sentences.zh: 欲令提綱而大道清，舉略而王法齊，其旨遠，其辭文，其言曲而中，其事肆而隱。

translations.literal: They intend that lifting the net clears the great Way; raising the outline aligns kingly law—intent remote, rhetoric ornate, words bent yet hitting center, affairs expansive yet hidden.
translations.idiomatic: Sparse wording masks vast regulatory intent.

sentences.zh: 通天下之志唯忠也，斷天下之疑唯文也，切天下之情唯遠也，彌天下之務唯大也，變無常體唯理也，非天下之賢聖，孰能與於斯！

translations.literal: Only loyalty penetrates all wills under heaven; only pattern cuts all doubts; only remoteness slices all emotions; only grandeur spans all tasks; only principle transforms without fixed form—who under heaven but sages shares such craft!
translations.idiomatic: Only canonical virtues decode law's cosmic scope.

sentences.zh: 夫刑而上者謂之道，刑而下者謂之器，化而裁之謂之格。

translations.literal: What transcends punishment is called Way; what lies below punishment is called implement; transforming and trimming it is called normative grid.
translations.idiomatic: Meta-law becomes Dao; applied law becomes instrument; adaptive rules become grids.

sentences.zh: 刑殺者是冬震曜之象，髡罪者似秋雕落之變，贖失者是春陽悔吝之疵之。

translations.literal: Execution resembles winter thunderbolt brilliance; shaved guilt resembles autumn leaf-fall; redeemed fault resembles spring-yang blemishes of regret.
translations.idiomatic: Capital punishment echoes winter thunder; mutilation echoes autumn decay; fines echo spring faults.

sentences.zh: 五刑成章，輒相依准，法律之義焉。

translations.literal: Five punishments forming chapters mutually rely—such is law's meaning.
translations.idiomatic: Five chapters interlock by design.

sentences.zh: 是時侍中盧珽、中書侍郎張華又表：「抄《新律》諸死罪條目，懸之亭傳，以示兆庶。

translations.literal: Then Palace Attendant Lu Ting and Secretariat Gentleman Zhang Hua memorialized: "Extract capital-crime articles from the New Statutes and hang them at courier lodges to show the myriad masses."
translations.idiomatic: Lu Ting and Zhang Hua proposed posting capital statutes at roadside stations.

sentences.zh: 」有詔從之。

translations.literal: " An edict approved.
translations.idiomatic: The throne agreed.

sentences.zh: 及劉頌為廷尉，頻表宜復肉刑，不見省，又上言曰：

translations.literal: When Liu Song became commandant of justice he repeatedly memorialized restoring corporal punishment without response; he again spoke:
translations.idiomatic: Liu Song renewed corporal-punishment petitions from the Ministry of Justice.

sentences.zh: 臣昔上行肉刑，從來積年，遂寢不論。

translations.literal: Your servant formerly promoted corporal punishment; years passed yet discussion slept.
translations.idiomatic: Years ago I urged corporal punishment—still tabled.

sentences.zh: 臣竊以為議者拘孝文之小仁，而輕違聖王之典刑，未詳之甚，莫過於此。

translations.literal: Your servant privately thinks debaters cling to Emperor Wen's petty kindness and lightly violate sage-king canonical punishments—nothing more ignorant.
translations.idiomatic: Critics indulge Wen's sentimental mercy and forsake classical mutilation.

sentences.zh: 今死刑重，故非命者眾；

translations.literal: Now capital punishment weighs heavily so unnatural deaths abound;
translations.idiomatic: Heavy capital statutes multiply wrongful deaths;

sentences.zh: 生刑輕，故罪不禁奸。

translations.literal: living punishments weigh lightly so crimes cannot restrain villainy.
translations.idiomatic: light labor sentences fail to deter wickedness.

sentences.zh: 所以然者，肉刑不用之所致也。

translations.literal: The reason is failing to use corporal punishments.
translations.idiomatic: Root cause: abandoning corporal options.

sentences.zh: 今為徒者，類性元惡不軌之族也，去家懸遠，作役山谷，饑寒切身，志不聊生，雖有廉士介者，苟慮不首死，則皆為盜賊，豈況本性奸凶無賴之徒乎！

translations.literal: Today labor convicts mostly stem from incorrigible clans; removed far from home toiling in mountains, hunger and cold grip them so life feels unbearable—even honest men, fearing death less than misery, turn bandit—how much more base villains!
translations.idiomatic: Exiled laborers—mostly habitual offenders—starve in mountains until even decent men become thieves.

sentences.zh: 又令徒富者輸財，解日歸家，乃無役之人也。

translations.literal: Moreover wealthy convicts buy release with property and return home—effectively avoiding labor.
translations.idiomatic: Rich inmates ransom release while poor ones rot in gangs.

sentences.zh: 貧者起為奸盜，又不制之虜也。

translations.literal: Poor men rise as robbers-thieves—another unchecked plague.
translations.idiomatic: Destitute laborers slide into theft without restraint.

sentences.zh: 不刑，則罪無所禁；

translations.literal: Without corporal punishment crimes cannot be barred;
translations.idiomatic: Without mutilation crime spreads unchecked;

sentences.zh: 不制，則群惡橫肆。

translations.literal: without restraint villain packs run rampant.
translations.idiomatic: without deterrence gangs rage openly.

sentences.zh: 為法若此，近不盡善也。

translations.literal: Law framed thus hardly reaches perfection.
translations.idiomatic: Such policy barely qualifies as sound.

sentences.zh: 是以徒亡日屬，賊盜日煩，亡之數者至有十數，得輒加刑，日益一歲，此為終身之徒也。

translations.literal: Therefore fugitives multiply daily; theft flourishes; escape counts reach dozens—each capture adds another year until lifetime labor results.
translations.idiomatic: Escalating escape penalties trap convicts in perpetual labor.

sentences.zh: 自顧反善無期，而災困逼身，其志亡思盜，勢不得息，事使之然也。

translations.literal: Seeing no hope of reform while disaster presses, minds plot theft with no rest—circumstances force it.
translations.idiomatic: Hopeless lifers hunt loot because circumstance leaves no choice.

sentences.zh: 古者用刑以止刑，今反於此。

translations.literal: Antiquity used punishments to end punishments—today reverses this.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient law ended crime through punishment; modern practice inverts it.

sentences.zh: 諸重犯亡者，發過三寸輒重髡之，此以刑生刑；

translations.literal: Serious fugitives whose hair grows past three inches receive repeated shaving—punishment breeding punishment;
translations.idiomatic: Recaptured rebels lose hair repeatedly—sentence spawning sentence;

sentences.zh: 加作一歲，此以徒生徒也。

translations.literal: adding another year labor produces labor breeding labor.
translations.idiomatic: stacked years breed endless labor.

sentences.zh: 亡者積多，系囚猥畜。

translations.literal: Escapes accumulate; dungeons swell.
translations.idiomatic: Jails overflow with repeat escapees.

sentences.zh: 議者曰囚不可不赦，復從而赦之，此為刑不制罪，法不勝奸。

translations.literal: Critics say prisoners cannot avoid amnesty—yet amnesty follows—this means punishments cannot master crime and law cannot defeat villainy.
translations.idiomatic: Endless amnesties admit law cannot defeat crime.

sentences.zh: 下知法之不勝，相聚而謀為不軌，月異而歲不同。

translations.literal: Inferiors knowing law inadequate gather plotting rebellion—monthly shifts yearly alter tactics.
translations.idiomatic: Criminals exploit legal weakness with evolving plots.

sentences.zh: 故自頃年以來，奸惡陵暴，所在充斥。

translations.literal: Thus recent years see villainy bullying truth everywhere.
translations.idiomatic: Recent seasons swarm with violent crime.

sentences.zh: 議者不深思此故，而曰肉刑於名忤聽，忤聽孰與賊盜不禁？

translations.literal: Critics never ponder this yet say corporal punishment offends hearing—which offends more: unpleasant names or unchecked theft?
translations.idiomatic: Cosmetic objection to mutilation ignores rampant robbery.

sentences.zh: 聖王之制肉刑，遠有深理，其事可得而言，非徒懲其畏剝割之痛而不為也，乃去其為惡之具，使夫奸人無用復肆其志，止奸絕本，理之盡也。

translations.literal: Sage kings devised corporal punishments with profound logic—not merely frightening men from cuts but removing tools of evil so villains cannot resume scheming—cutting roots ends villainy utterly.
translations.idiomatic: Mutilation removes criminal capacity, not merely fear.

sentences.zh: 亡者刖足，無所用復亡。

translations.literal: Fugitives lose feet—cannot flee again.
translations.idiomatic: Footless escapees cannot run;

sentences.zh: 盜者截手，無所用復盜。

translations.literal: thieves lose hands—cannot steal again;
translations.idiomatic: handless thieves cannot steal;

sentences.zh: 淫者割其勢，理亦如之。

translations.literal: adulterers lose organs—same reasoning.
translations.idiomatic: castration follows rapists likewise.

sentences.zh: 除惡塞源，莫善於此，非徒然也。

translations.literal: Eliminating evil at its source—nothing superior—no idle gesture.
translations.idiomatic: Amputation eradicates evil at source.

sentences.zh: 此等已刑之後，便各歸家，父母妻子，共相養恤，不流離于塗路。

translations.literal: After punishment convicts return home—parents, wives, children mutually sustain—not drifting roadside.
translations.idiomatic: Maimed offenders stay home supported by kin.

sentences.zh: 有今之困，創愈可役，上准古制，隨宜業作，雖已刑殘，不為虛棄，而所患都塞，又生育繁阜之道自若也。

translations.literal: Despite today's hardships wounds heal into usable labor; matching antiquity they take suitable work—though maimed they are not wasted castoffs; worries halt while population still breeds.
translations.idiomatic: Scarred workers still tend fields under supervised labor; society keeps producing.

sentences.zh: 今宜取死刑之限輕，及三犯逃亡淫盜，悉以肉刑代之。

translations.literal: Now take lighter capital cases and thrice-escaped lewd bandits—replace all with corporal sentences.
translations.idiomatic: Demote borderline capitals and chronic sex-thieves to mutilation.

sentences.zh: 其三歲刑以下，已自杖罰遣，又宜制其罰數，使有常限，不得減此。

translations.literal: Punishments three years and below already suffer cane fines—further fix stroke counts with fixed limits never reducible.
translations.idiomatic: Cap sub-three-year caning with mandatory floors.

sentences.zh: 其有宜重者，又任之官長。

translations.literal: When heavier needs arise, local chiefs may adjust.
translations.idiomatic: Superiors may add weight case by case.

sentences.zh: 應四五歲刑者，皆髡笞，笞至一百，稍行，使各有差，悉不復居作。

translations.literal: Those fit for four- or five-year terms receive shaving plus flogging to one hundred strokes in stages—no more corvée residence.
translations.idiomatic: Mid felonies become shave-plus-cane without prison labor.

sentences.zh: 然後刑不復生刑，徒不復生徒，而殘體為戳，終身作誡。

translations.literal: Then punishment no longer begets punishment nor labor begets labor—maimed bodies stand as lifelong warnings.
translations.idiomatic: Stopping punishment spirals, mutilation educates forever.

sentences.zh: 人見其痛，畏而不犯，必數倍於今。

translations.literal: People seeing pain fear doubly more than today.
translations.idiomatic: Visible agony deters more than remote labor.

sentences.zh: 且為惡者隨發被刑，去其為惡之具，此為諸已刑者皆良士也，豈與全其為奸之手足，而蹴居必死之窮地同哉！

translations.literal: Evil-doers mutilated on capture lose their tools—such men become good subjects—unlike leaving villain limbs intact to corner them toward death.
translations.idiomatic: Timely mutilation redeems; intact limbs drive desperados.

sentences.zh: 而猶曰肉刑不可用，臣竊以為不識務之甚也。

translations.literal: Yet voices say corporal law cannot apply—your servant deems that utter policy blindness.
translations.idiomatic: Denying mutilation misunderstands statecraft.

sentences.zh: 臣昔常侍左右，數聞明詔，謂肉刑宜用，事便於政。

translations.literal: Your servant once attended the throne often hearing edicts that corporal punishment benefits administration.
translations.idiomatic: Court whispers already endorsed corporal law.

sentences.zh: 願陛下信獨見之斷，使夫能者得奉聖慮，行之於今。

translations.literal: May Your Majesty trust this lonely resolve and let able men enact sage worry in our age.
translations.idiomatic: Trust the policy and commission experts to codify it.

sentences.zh: 比填溝壑，冀見太平。

translations.literal: I am ready to fill ditches and hope to glimpse great peace.
translations.idiomatic: I offer my life to see tranquil rule.

sentences.zh: 《周禮》三赦三宥，施於老幼悼耄，黔黎不屬逮者，此非為惡之所出，故刑法逆舍而宥之。

translations.literal: Zhou Rites' three pardons and three mercies cover old young and infirm—commoners not subject to capture—because evil does not stem from them, so law pauses and forgives.
translations.idiomatic: Rites spare juveniles and senility because guilt rarely originates there.

sentences.zh: 至於自非此族，犯罪則必刑而無赦，此政之理也。

translations.literal: All outside these groups, once guilty, must be punished without mercy—this is governance's pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Adult repeat offenders receive no quarter.

sentences.zh: 暨至後世，以時嶮多難，因赦解結，權以行之，又不以寬罪人也。

translations.literal: Later ages, times treacherous, used amnesties to untie knots—expedient, not true leniency toward culprits.
translations.idiomatic: Later dynasties amnestied for crisis control, not mercy.

sentences.zh: 至今恆以罪積獄繁，赦以散之，是以赦愈數而獄愈塞，如此不已，將至不勝。

translations.literal: Now crimes pile, jails jam, amnesties scatter them—so more amnesties clog courts—endlessly unsustainable.
translations.idiomatic: Frequent amnesties stuffed prisons worse.

sentences.zh: 原其所由，內刑不用之故也。

translations.literal: Trace the root—because corporal law lies unused.
translations.idiomatic: No mutilation forces amnesty bloat.

sentences.zh: 今行肉刑，非徒不積，且為惡無具則奸息。

translations.literal: Enact corporal punishments—not only unclog courts but deprive evil of tools.
translations.idiomatic: Mutilation both empties jails and removes criminal means.

sentences.zh: 去此二端，獄不得繁，故無取於數赦，於政體勝矣。

translations.literal: Remove these two issues—dungeons need not crowd; skip serial amnesties; policy prevails.
translations.idiomatic: With mutilation plus deterrence, amnesties become unnecessary.

sentences.zh: 疏上，又不見省。

translations.literal: Memorial up—again ignored.
translations.idiomatic: The throne again shelved Liu Song.

sentences.zh: 至惠帝之世，政出群下，每有疑獄，各立私情，刑法不定，獄訟繁滋。

translations.literal: By Emperor Hui's reign power scattered below; each doubtful case nursed private bias; punishments wavered; suits multiplied.
translations.idiomatic: Hui's court factionalized justice and docket chaos exploded.

sentences.zh: 尚書裴頠表陳之曰：

translations.literal: Minister Pei Wei memorialized saying:
translations.idiomatic: Pei Wei then submitted:

sentences.zh: 夫天下之事多塗，非一司之所管；

translations.literal: Affairs under heaven run many paths—not one office may govern all.
translations.idiomatic: State business spans ministries needing division of labor.

sentences.zh: 中才之情易擾，賴恆制而後定。

translations.literal: Middling talents are easily perturbed; they rely on constant systems to settle.
translations.idiomatic: Average officials need fixed rules to stay calm.

sentences.zh: 先王知其所以然也，是以辨方分職，為之准局。

translations.literal: Former kings knew this, therefore they divided regions and tasks into measured scopes.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient kings assigned jurisdictions deliberately.

sentences.zh: 准局既立，各掌其務，刑賞相稱，輕重無二，故下聽有常，群吏安業也。

translations.literal: Once scopes stand each manages its charge; reward and punishment match; light and heavy stay even—hence subordinates listen consistently and clerks find peace.
translations.idiomatic: Clear jurisdiction balances incentives and steadies clerks.

sentences.zh: 舊宮掖陵廟有水火毀傷之變，然後尚書乃躬自奔赴，其非此也，皆止于郎令史而已。

translations.literal: Formerly only after palace, tumulus, or temple fire or flood would the Minister himself rush; otherwise only bureau gentlemen handled it.
translations.idiomatic: Catastrophes alone drew ministers personally; minor roof checks stayed with clerks.

sentences.zh: 刑罰所加，各有常刑。

translations.literal: Punishment applications each had regular statutes.
translations.idiomatic: Each offense had a fixed penalty ladder.

sentences.zh: 去元康四年，大風之後，廟闕屋瓦有數枚傾落，免太常荀寓。

translations.literal: In fourth year of Yuankang, after great wind, several temple eaves-tiles fell—Minister of Ceremonies Xun Yu was dismissed.
translations.idiomatic: Yuankang 4 windstorm tiles toppled; Xun Yu took the fall.

sentences.zh: 于時以嚴詔所譴，莫敢據正。

translations.literal: At the time harsh edict blame—none dared argue rectitude.
translations.idiomatic: Harsh edicts silenced dissent.

sentences.zh: 然內外之意，僉謂事輕責重，有違于常。

translations.literal: Court consensus judged fault light yet punishment heavy—contrary to precedent.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone felt penalties disproportionate.

sentences.zh: 會五年二月有大風，主者懲懼前事。

translations.literal: When fifth year second month brought another gale, officials dreaded repeating prior ordeal.
translations.idiomatic: Month-two winds next year made clerks paranoid.

sentences.zh: 臣新拜尚書始三日，本曹尚書有疾，權令兼出，按行蘭台。

translations.literal: Your servant had just become Minister three days; chief minister fell ill so your servant temporarily inspected Orchid Terrace.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Wei briefly supervised inspections.

sentences.zh: 主者乃瞻望阿棟之間，求索瓦之不正者，得棟上瓦小邪十五處。

translations.literal: Inspectors stared between beams hunting crooked tiles—finding fifteen slightly skewed ridge tiles.
translations.idiomatic: Teams counted fifteen slightly misaligned ridge tiles.

sentences.zh: 或是始瓦時邪，蓋不足言，風起倉卒，台官更往，太常按行，不及得周，文書未至之頃，便競相禁止。

translations.literal: Perhaps masons laid them crooked originally—hardly worth mentioning—yet sudden winds sent Terrace officers and Minister of Ceremonies scrambling incomplete inspections while paperwork lagged—everyone raced to embargo repairs.
translations.idiomatic: Minor skew blamed on builders yet panic triggered blanket bans mid-inspection.

sentences.zh: 臣以權兼暫出，出還便罷，不復得窮其事。

translations.literal: Your servant held temporary duty—returning ended authority—could not pursue detail.
translations.idiomatic: Acting supervisors lost mandate once rotated.

sentences.zh: 而本曹據執，卻問無已。

translations.literal: Yet home bureau clung stubbornly questioning endlessly.
translations.idiomatic: Permanent staff kept interrogating Ceremonies.

sentences.zh: 臣時具加解遣，而主者畏咎，不從臣言，禁止太常，復興刑獄。

translations.literal: Your servant explained dismissal yet chiefs feared blame—ignored advice—embargoed Minister of Ceremonies reopening trials.
translations.idiomatic: Despite Pei Wei's orders, terrified clerks prosecuted ritual ministers again.

sentences.zh: 昔漢氏有盜廟玉環者，文帝欲族誅，釋之但處以死刑，曰：「若侵長陵一抔土，何以復加？

translations.literal: Former Han stole temple jade rings—Emperor Wen wished clan execution but Zhang Shi sentenced death alone saying "If encroaching Changling by one handful of soil—what worse penalty remains?"
translations.idiomatic: Han precedent: Zhang Shiji limited tomb theft to capital guilt.

sentences.zh: 」文帝從之。

translations.literal: " Emperor Wen obeyed.
translations.idiomatic: Wendi accepted.

sentences.zh: 大晉垂制，深惟經遠，山陵不封，園邑不飾，墓而不墳，同乎山壤，是以丘阪存其陳草，使齊乎中原矣。

translations.literal: Great Jin's enduring system reveres distance—imperial tumuli unsealed, park estates unadorned, graves flush with soil like hills—wild grass marks resting kings matching plain earth.
translations.idiomatic: Jin tombs lie low without mounds—indistinguishable hills.

sentences.zh: 雖陵兆尊嚴，唯毀發然後族之，此古典也。

translations.literal: Though tombs inspire awe only excavation warrants clan execution—classical rule.
translations.idiomatic: Grand Jin reserves clan slaughter for actual tomb breach.

sentences.zh: 若登踐犯損，失盡敬之道，事止刑罪可也。

translations.literal: If treading or bruising loses reverence, ordinary penal guilt suffices.
translations.idiomatic: Footprints or careless damage merit regular sentencing only.

sentences.zh: 去八年，奴聽教加誣周龍燒草，廷尉遂奏族龍，一門八口並命。

translations.literal: Eight years ago a slave obeying orders falsely accused Zhou Long burning grass—the commandant memorialized clan execution—eight mouths perished.
translations.idiomatic: Eight years prior a framed Zhou Long nearly lost eight kin.

sentences.zh: 會龍獄翻，然後得免。

translations.literal: Only when Long's case overturned did they escape.
translations.idiomatic: Retrial freed them.

sentences.zh: 考之情理，准之前訓，所處實重。

translations.literal: Measured against reason and ancient exempla—the sentence was harsh.
translations.idiomatic: That verdict exceeded proportional justice.

sentences.zh: 今年八月，陵上荊一枝圍七寸二分者被斫，司徒太常，奔走道路，雖知事小，而案劾難測，搔擾驅馳，各競免負，於今太常禁止未解。

translations.literal: This eighth month someone cut a seven-inch-two-branch vine on the tomb mound—Minister and Ceremonies raced roads knowing matter petty yet unpredictable prosecution harassed everyone avoiding blame—Ceremonies offices remain embargoed.
translations.idiomatic: Petty branch-cutting triggered another Ceremonies inquisition still open.

sentences.zh: 近日太祝署失火，燒屋三間半。

translations.literal: Recently Archivist Directorate fire burned three and a half rooms.
translations.idiomatic: Last week the Blessing office fire consumed half the annex.

sentences.zh: 署在廟北，隔道在重牆之內，又即已滅，頻為詔旨所問。

translations.literal: It sits north of temple inside double walls—already extinguished—yet edicts repeatedly inquire.
translations.idiomatic: Fire stayed inside temple walls yet palace demanded endless reports.

sentences.zh: 主者以詔旨使問頻繁，便責尚書不即案行，輒禁止，尚書免，皆在法外。

translations.literal: Handlers, citing frequent edict inquiries, blamed Minister for slow inspection—again embargoed Minister—dismissals landed outside statutory bounds.
translations.idiomatic: Clerics punished ministers extra-legally for delayed surveys.

sentences.zh: 刑書之文有限，而舛違之故無方，故有臨時議處之制，誠不能皆得循常也。

translations.literal: Statute text is finite, yet causes of error know no limit—hence the system of ad hoc deliberation; one cannot in every case follow a constant rule.
translations.idiomatic: Because written law cannot cover every factual twist, judges need emergency procedures that sometimes break the usual rulebook.

sentences.zh: 至於此等，皆為過當，每相逼迫，不得以理，上替聖朝畫一之德，下損崇禮大臣之望。

translations.literal: As for these cases, all have exceeded the proper measure, each side pressing the other, unable to apply reason—above it undermines the sagely court’s virtue of uniform standards, below it injures the expectation that great ministers be honored in ritual.
translations.idiomatic: These overreactions in tomb cases undercut the court’s commitment to one law for all and embarrass senior ministers who stand for proper ceremony.

sentences.zh: 臣愚以為犯陵上草木，不應乃用同產異刑之制。

translations.literal: Your servant thinks that treading on plants above an imperial tumulus should not call forth the system of different punishments for those who share the same birth.
translations.idiomatic: Trampling graveyard growth should not trigger the same draconian kin-punishment statutes used for true desecration.

sentences.zh: 按行奏劾，應有定準，相承務重，體例遂虧。

translations.literal: Investigations and impeachments ought to have fixed standards; generation after generation they pursued severity, and the body of precedent was thus injured.
translations.idiomatic: Inspections and indictments need stable yardsticks, not an ever-harsher drift that warps precedent.

sentences.zh: 或因余事，得容淺深。

translations.literal: Sometimes, by way of other matters, one may accommodate lighter or deeper guilt.
translations.idiomatic: Collateral issues can still adjust how heavy a sentence feels.

sentences.zh: 頠雖有此表，曲議猶不止。

translations.literal: Although Pei had submitted this memorial, captious side-debates still did not cease.
translations.idiomatic: Even after Pei Wei’s paper, carping continued.

sentences.zh: 時劉頌為三公尚書，又上疏曰：

translations.literal: At the time Liu Song, as Minister of the Three Dukes, again submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: Liu Song, serving as the Three Excellencies’ overseer, then added this argument:

sentences.zh: 自近世以來，法漸多門，令甚不一。

translations.literal: From recent generations onward, law has gradually acquired many gates, and edicts are extremely inconsistent.
translations.idiomatic: Recent decades multiplied alternate legal “doors” and clashing edicts.

sentences.zh: 臣今備掌刑斷，職思其憂，謹具啟聞。

translations.literal: Your servant now fully manages criminal decisions; pondering this worry, I respectfully lay it before you.
translations.idiomatic: As the minister now holding capital jurisdiction, I must report my concern.

sentences.zh: 臣竊伏惟陛下為政，每盡善，故事求曲當，則例不得直；

translations.literal: Your servant humbly reflects that when Your Majesty governs, every time you seek a perfect match to circumstance; if in precedents and examples you seek a perfect match, the pattern cannot stay straight.
translations.idiomatic: Bending every case to feel perfectly tailored breaks consistent rules.

sentences.zh: 盡善，故法不得全。

translations.literal: Because you seek perfection, the law cannot remain whole.
translations.idiomatic: The quest to perfect each outcome shreds a unified code.

sentences.zh: 何則？

translations.literal: Why is that?
translations.idiomatic: Why?

sentences.zh: 夫法者，固以盡理為法，而上求盡善，則諸下牽文就意，以赴主之所許，是以法不得全。

translations.literal: Law by its nature takes exhausting principle to be law, but if superiors demand perfection, all subordinates twist the text to match what the ruler likes—therefore the law cannot remain whole.
translations.idiomatic: When clerks stretch clauses to match imperial whim, the statute fractures.

sentences.zh: 刑書徵文，徵文必有乖於情聽之斷，而上安于曲當，故執平者因文可引，則生二端。

translations.literal: Criminal writings cite text; citing text necessarily diverges from judgments based on emotional hearings—yet superiors settle for devious fitness, so those who hold balance, wherever text can be stretched, produce paired interpretations.
translations.idiomatic: Literal argument forks whenever rulers reward clever readings over predictable ones.

sentences.zh: 是法多門，令不一，則吏不知所守，下不知所避。

translations.literal: Thus law has many gates and edicts do not agree—clerks know not what to guard and commoners know not what to avoid.
translations.idiomatic: A fractured code leaves officials and subjects guessing.

sentences.zh: 奸偽者因法之多門，以售其情，所欲淺深，苟斷不一，則居上者難以檢下，於是事同議異，獄犴不平，有傷於法。

translations.literal: The crafty exploit law’s many gates to peddle their angle; if verdict depth varies at whim, those above cannot inspect those below—same facts spawn divergent opinions and unequal prisons, harming the law.
translations.idiomatic: Sharp lawyers shop forums until punishments become arbitrary.

sentences.zh: 古人有言：「人主詳，其政荒；

translations.literal: The ancients said: ‘When the lord is meticulous, his government withers;’
translations.idiomatic: Antiquity warned that micromanaging rulers paralyze government;

sentences.zh: 人主期，其事理。

translations.literal: ‘when the lord sets expectation, affairs become ordered.’
translations.idiomatic: while rulers who demand predictable outcomes keep affairs tidy.

sentences.zh: 」詳匪他，盡善則法傷，故其政荒也。

translations.literal: ‘Meticulous’ means nothing else—seeking perfection injures law, hence government withers.
translations.idiomatic: Perfectionism corrodes legal uniformity.

sentences.zh: 期者輕重之當，雖不厭情，苟入于文，則循而行之，故其事理也。

translations.literal: Expectation means fitness of light and heavy; though it may not satisfy hearts, if it enters the text, follow and execute it—therefore affairs become ordered.
translations.idiomatic: Codified proportionality beats sentimental tailoring.

sentences.zh: 夫善用法者，忍違情不厭聽之斷，輕重雖不允人心，經於凡覽，若不可行，法乃得直。

translations.literal: Those skilled at using law endure violating emotion to preserve consistent hearings; though severity may not please popular hearts, when ordinary review thinks it unenforceable, only then does law stand upright.
translations.idiomatic: Sound adjudication accepts unpopular but printed sentences.

sentences.zh: 又君臣之分，各有所司。

translations.literal: Moreover lord and minister each has his duty.
translations.idiomatic: Sovereign and minister occupy distinct roles.

sentences.zh: 法欲必奉，故令主者守文；

translations.literal: Because law must be obeyed, instruct specialists to guard the text.
translations.idiomatic: Line judges must cling to written clauses.

sentences.zh: 理有窮塞，故使大臣釋滯；

translations.literal: Because principle may block, let great ministers release the obstruction.
translations.idiomatic: Senior ministers settle statutory deadlocks.

sentences.zh: 事有時宜，故人主權斷。

translations.literal: Because affairs have timely fitness, the human lord wields authority to decide.
translations.idiomatic: Only the emperor handles timely exceptions.

sentences.zh: 主者守文，若釋之執犯蹕之平也；

translations.literal: Specialists guarding text resemble Zhang Shi holding fast to the equal verdict on breaking the imperial avenue cordon.
translations.idiomatic: Low judges mirror Zhang Shi’s refusal to bend the carriage-interdiction rule.

sentences.zh: 大臣釋滯，若公孫弘斷郭解之獄也；

translations.literal: Great ministers releasing obstruction resemble Gongsun Hong deciding Guo Jie’s prison case.
translations.idiomatic: Senior jurists untangle cases the way Gongsun Hong handled Guo Jie.

sentences.zh: 人主權斷，若漢祖戮丁公之為也。

translations.literal: Lordly authority deciding resembles Han founder executing Ding Gong’s breach of loyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Royal discretion recalls Gaozu killing Ding Gong despite merit.

sentences.zh: 天下萬事，自非斯格重為，故不近似此類，不得出以意妄議，其餘皆以律令從事。

translations.literal: All matters under heaven—unless they are not of this pattern as weighty exceptions—may not be aired by whim outside statute; all the rest follow statutes and edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Outside rare imperial prerogative, every matter stays inside codified law.

sentences.zh: 然後法信於下，人聽不惑，吏不容奸，可以言政。

translations.literal: Only then does law win trust below, popular hearing stays unconfused, clerks cannot harbor deceit, and one may speak of government.
translations.idiomatic: Predictable law earns trust, foils bribery, and makes governance possible.

sentences.zh: 人主軌斯格以責群下，大臣小吏各守其局，則法一矣。

translations.literal: The lord uses this pattern to demand performance from all below; great ministers and petty clerks each guard their station—then law is one.
translations.idiomatic: When ruler and ranks stay inside fixed roles, uniformity returns.

sentences.zh: 古人有言：「善為政者，看人設教。

translations.literal: The ancients said: ‘Good governors tailor teaching to their people.’
translations.idiomatic: Tradition says wise rulers teach according to their people’s needs.

sentences.zh: 」看人設教，制法之謂也。

translations.literal: "Tailoring teaching to people” means making law.
translations.idiomatic: That is how positive law is born.

sentences.zh: 又曰：「隨時之宜」，當務之謂也。

translations.literal: They also said: ‘Suit the season’s fitness’—that is seizing the present task.
translations.idiomatic: “Suit the times” means handling what the moment requires.

sentences.zh: 然則看人隨時，在大量也，而制其法。

translations.literal: Therefore watching people and seasons lies in the grand measure, and with that you frame the statutes.
translations.idiomatic: People- and time-surveying inform the code’s great design.

sentences.zh: 法軌既定則行之，行之信如四時，執之堅如金石，群吏豈得在成制之內，復稱隨時之宜，傍引看人設教，以亂政典哉！

translations.literal: Once the legal track is set, carry it out; its faithfulness is like the four seasons, its firmness like metal and stone—how can host of clerics, within completed systems, again invoke timely fitness, sidelong quote tailored teaching, and disorder the government’s canons!
translations.idiomatic: After promulgation, law must run like clockwork; bureau ranks may not re-open “flexible” teaching to dilute the code.

sentences.zh: 何則？

translations.literal: Why?
translations.idiomatic: Why not?

sentences.zh: 始制之初，固已看人而隨時矣。

translations.literal: At the first founding, the system already watched people and followed the times.
translations.idiomatic: Drafters already embedded people and season into the text.

sentences.zh: 今若設法未盡當，則宜改之。

translations.literal: If the law as set is not yet right, it is right to change it.
translations.idiomatic: If the code misfits, amend it formally.

sentences.zh: 若謂已善，不得盡以為制，而使奉用之司公得出入以差輕重也。

translations.literal: If you say it is already good, you may not take the whole as system yet let implementing offices in and out to shift light and heavy at will.
translations.idiomatic: Do not call the code perfect while letting clerks improvise sentence weight.

sentences.zh: 夫人君所與天下共者，法也。

translations.literal: What the lord shares with all under heaven is the law.
translations.idiomatic: Sovereign and realm share the same published law.

sentences.zh: 已令四海，不可以不信以為教，方求天下之不慢，不可繩以不信之法。

translations.literal: An edict already commands the four seas—you cannot teach incredibility; seeking not to let the realm despise you, you cannot bind them with untrusted statutes.
translations.idiomatic: Credibility is the foundation of obedience.

sentences.zh: 且先識有言，人至遇而不可欺也。

translations.literal: Moreover earlier wisdom says even clever humans meeting sagacity cannot be deceived.
translations.idiomatic: Wise rulers admit plain facts humans cannot fake forever.

sentences.zh: 不謂平時背法意斷，不勝百姓願也。

translations.literal: It does not mean ordinarily betraying legal intent in verdicts yet satisfying popular expectation.
translations.idiomatic: Law cannot chase applause case by case.

sentences.zh: 上古議事以制，不為刑辟。

translations.literal: High antiquity decided affairs by deliberation, not by carving punishments.
translations.idiomatic: Earliest ages judged case-by-case before codification;

sentences.zh: 夏殷及周，書法象魏。

translations.literal: Xia, Yin, and Zhou hung written law on the signal towers.
translations.idiomatic: Three dynasties posted statutes on watchtower gates.

sentences.zh: 三代之君齊聖，然咸棄曲當之妙鑒，而任徵文之直准，非聖有殊，所遇異也。

translations.literal: Those generations’ lords were uniformly sagely, yet all abandoned ad hoc perfectionism and relied on textual yardsticks—not because sages differed but circumstances did.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient kings preferred predictable text over improvised mercy.

sentences.zh: 今論時敦樸，不及中古，而執平者欲適情之所安，自托於議事以制。

translations.literal: Speaking of our age’s honesty, it cannot match middle antiquity, yet balance-holders wish to settle sentiment where convenient, hiding behind deliberative justice.
translations.idiomatic: Today's mediocrity cannot uphold feudal informal justice.

sentences.zh: 臣竊以為聽言則美，論理則違。

translations.literal: Your servant thinks such speech sounds lovely yet violates coherent principle.
translations.idiomatic: Romanticizing discretionary justice contradicts stable governance.

sentences.zh: 然天下至大，事務眾雜，時有不得悉循文如令。

translations.literal: Yet the realm is vast and affairs numerous—sometimes one cannot wholly follow text like edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Mass society produces corner cases beyond codification.

sentences.zh: 故臣謂宜立格為限，使主者守文，死生以之，不敢錯思于成制之外，以差輕重，則法恆全。

translations.literal: Therefore your servant proposes erecting grids as limits: specialists guard text; life and death depend on it—they dare not wander imagination beyond settled systems to tweak severity—then law stays constantly whole.
translations.idiomatic: Publish sentencing grids so clerks cannot freelance aggravation.

sentences.zh: 事無正據，名例不及，大臣論當，以釋不滯，則事無閡。

translations.literal: When affairs lack direct textual proof and general principles do not reach them, great ministers debate fitness to release blockage—then affairs lack obstruction.
translations.idiomatic: Senior councils settle gaps statutes omit.

sentences.zh: 至如非常之斷，出法賞罰，若漢祖戮楚臣之私己，封趙氏之無功，唯人主專之，非奉職之臣所得擬議。

translations.literal: As for extraordinary judgments or rewards exceeding statute—like Han founder killing Chu ministers for private motives or enfeoffing Lady Zhao without merit—only the lord monopolizes such acts; duty clerks may not emulate.
translations.idiomatic: Royal exceptionalism stays outside bureaucratic precedent.

sentences.zh: 然後情求傍請之跡絕，似是而非之奏塞，此蓋齊法之大准也。

translations.literal: Then tracks of emotional lobbying vanish and sophistries resembling truth clog no longer—this aligns law’s grand norms.
translations.idiomatic: Ending petition warfare restores systemic fairness.

sentences.zh: 主者小吏，處事無常。

translations.literal: Chief clerks and petty aides discharge affairs without constant rule.
translations.idiomatic: Low clerks oscillate unpredictably.

sentences.zh: 何則？

translations.literal: Why?
translations.idiomatic: Why?

sentences.zh: 無情則法徒克，有情則撓法。

translations.literal: Without sentiment law merely conquers; with sentiment law bends.
translations.idiomatic: Cold law alienates; sympathetic law corrupts.

sentences.zh: 積克似無私，然乃所以得其私，又恆所岨以衛其身。

translations.literal: Persistent severity seems selfless yet captures private advantage while forever stonewalling self-protection.
translations.idiomatic: Harsh judges cloak selfish safety.

sentences.zh: 斷當恆克，世謂盡公，時一曲法，乃所不疑。

translations.literal: Verdicts constantly harsh the age calls utterly just; occasional laxity raises no suspicion.
translations.idiomatic: Callous benches earn praise; mercy invites scrutiny.

sentences.zh: 故人君不善倚深似公之斷，而責守文如令之奏，然後得為有檢，此又平法之一端也。

translations.literal: Thus wise lords should not rely on severity posing as fairness yet demand submissions guarding text like edicts—only then may oversight exist—another facet of balanced law.
translations.idiomatic: Rulers must prize textual petitions over performative cruelty.

sentences.zh: 夫出法權制，指施一事，厭情合聽，可適耳目，誠有臨時當意之快，勝於徵文不允人心也。

translations.literal: Extra-statutory authoritative rulings address single incidents, pleasing ears and sentiment—indeed there is momentary satisfaction finer than textual verdicts that fail hearts.
translations.idiomatic: Ad hoc rulings seduce with empathy yet undermine precedent.

sentences.zh: 然起為經制，經年施用，恆得一而失十。

translations.literal: Yet turning them into standing practice applied year after year usually gains one benefit yet loses ten.
translations.idiomatic: Codifying improvisation yields tiny gains and systemic harm.

sentences.zh: 故小有所得者，必大有所失；

translations.literal: Therefore small gain implies large loss;
translations.idiomatic: Petty wins precede major losses;

sentences.zh: 近有所漏者，必遠有所苞。

translations.literal: near omission implies distant engulfment.
translations.idiomatic: local loopholes widen.

sentences.zh: 故諳事識體者，善權輕重，不以小害大，不以近妨遠。

translations.literal: Therefore those knowing affairs and grasping forms weigh advantages—never harming the great for the small nor distant for near.
translations.idiomatic: Seasoned jurists weigh systemic harm.

sentences.zh: 忍曲當之近適，以全簡直之大准。

translations.literal: They tolerate imperfect near fits to preserve broad straightforward norms.
translations.idiomatic: Near-term unfairness sometimes preserves long fairness.

sentences.zh: 不牽於凡聽之所安，必守徵文以正例。

translations.literal: They are not dragged by popular comfort yet cling to textual proofs that affirm precedent.
translations.idiomatic: Judges anchor doctrine despite applause.

sentences.zh: 每臨其事，恆禦此心以決斷，此又法之大概也。

translations.literal: Whenever confronting affairs they discipline mind by this rule—again law’s general tenor.
translations.idiomatic: Every bench decision should echo this discipline.

sentences.zh: 又律法斷罪，皆當以法律令正文，若無正文，依附名例斷之，其正文名例所不及，皆勿論。

translations.literal: Moreover statutes condemning crimes must rely on statute-edict main texts; where main texts lack, attach to general principles; where principles omit matters, do not discuss guilt.
translations.idiomatic: No conviction without positive statute or general-part analogy.

sentences.zh: 法吏以上，所執不同，得為異議。

translations.literal: Legal officers of fifth rank and above may lodge dissenting readings.
translations.idiomatic: Senior jurists may dispute interpretations.

sentences.zh: 如律之文，守法之官，唯當奉用律令。

translations.literal: Per statute text, officers guarding law must reverently apply statutes and edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Line judges enforce codified law.

sentences.zh: 至於法律之內，所見不同，乃得為異議也。

translations.literal: Only differing opinions inside statute-edict texts qualify as dissent.
translations.idiomatic: Dissent stays intra-statutory.

sentences.zh: 今限法曹郎令史，意有不同為駁，唯得論釋法律，以正所斷，不得援求諸外，論隨時之宜，以明法官守局之分。

translations.literal: Now restrict Director-of-Law gentlemen and clerks: dissent notes must exegete statute alone to straighten verdict—cannot cite outside expedients or seasonal convenience—clarifying jurists’ jurisdictions.
translations.idiomatic: Dissents cite law books only, never policy memos.

sentences.zh: 詔下其事。

translations.literal: An edict forwarded the matter.
translations.idiomatic: The throne circulated Liu Song’s memo.

sentences.zh: 侍中、太宰、汝南王亮奏以為：「夫禮以訓世，而法以整俗，理化之本，事實由之。

translations.literal: Palace Attendant, Grand Tutor, Prince of Runan Sima Liang memorialized: "Ritual trains the world while law straightens custom—the roots of transformation lie therein.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Sima Liang endorsed Liu Song:

sentences.zh: 若斷不斷，常輕重隨意，則王憲不一，人無所錯矣。

translations.literal: If verdicts hesitate and severity swings by whim, royal authority lacks unity and people cannot orient.
translations.idiomatic: Inconsistent punishment destroys predictability.

sentences.zh: 故觀人設教，在上之舉；

translations.literal: Therefore tailoring teaching to people rests with superiors;
translations.idiomatic: Custom policy flows from the throne;

sentences.zh: 守文直法，臣吏之節也。

translations.literal: guarding text and law exemplifies ministerial duty.
translations.idiomatic: judges enforce statutes faithfully.

sentences.zh: 臣以去太康八年，隨事異議。

translations.literal: Your servant thinks since Taikang eighth year each matter drew differing opinions.
translations.idiomatic: Since Taikang 8 cases wandered off-script.

sentences.zh: 周懸象魏之書，漢詠畫一之法，誠以法與時共，義不可二。

translations.literal: Zhou hung tower writings; Han praised unified brushstrokes—law must march with time yet principle cannot split.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient parallels demand singular codes.

sentences.zh: 今法素定，而法為議，則有所開長，以為宜如頌所啟，為永久之制。

translations.literal: Now law is settled yet debate continues—this opens loopholes; your servant thinks Liu Song’s proposal should become perpetual rule.
translations.idiomatic: Codify Liu Song’s plea permanently.

sentences.zh: 」於是門下屬三公曰：「昔先王議事以制，自中古以來，執法斷事，既以立法，誠不宜復求法外小善也。

translations.literal: " Thereupon Chancellery instructed the Three Dukes: "Ancient kings deliberated cases before carving punishments; since middle antiquity executing offices judge by enacted law—it truly should not again pursue petty kindness outside law.
translations.idiomatic: Edict tells ministers discretionary mercy ends.

sentences.zh: 若常以善奪法，則人逐善而不忌法，其害甚於無法也。

translations.literal: If kindness routinely overrides law, people chase kindness without fearing law—harm exceeds having no law.
translations.idiomatic: Mercy metastasizes worse than legal vacuum.

sentences.zh: 案啟事，欲令法令斷一，事無二門，郎令史已下，應復出法駁案，隨事以聞也。」

translations.literal: Examining the memorial wishes verdict unity with single gate—clerks below directors may submit statutory dissents case-by-case upward.
translations.idiomatic: Implement hierarchical dissent procedure.

sentences.zh: 及于江左，元帝為丞相時，朝廷草創，議斷不循法律，人立異議，高下無狀。

translations.literal: East of the Yangzi, when Emperor Yuan was Chancellor, court beginnings improvised verdicts outside law—every man voiced dissent; severity lacked measure.
translations.idiomatic: Jin survival court judged without statutes.

sentences.zh: 主簿熊遠奏曰：「禮以崇善，法以閑非，故禮有常典，法有常防，人知惡而無邪心。

translations.literal: Registrar Xiong Yuan memorialized: "Ritual elevates good; law fences evil—therefore ritual has constant canon, law constant guard—people know evil yet lack wicked hearts.
translations.idiomatic: Xiong Yuan pleaded for statute supremacy:

sentences.zh: 是以周建象魏之制，漢創畫一之法，故能闡弘大道，以至刑厝。

translations.literal: Hence Zhou erected tower postings and Han forged unified methods—thus they spread great ways until punishments lay idle.
translations.idiomatic: Tower statutes enabled peaceful ages.

sentences.zh: 律令之作，由來尚矣。

translations.literal: Statutes and edicts emerged long ago.
translations.idiomatic: Written law has ancient pedigree.

sentences.zh: 經賢智，曆夷險，隨時斟酌，最為周備。

translations.literal: Sages refined them through difficulty and ease, adapting as needed—most comprehensive.
translations.idiomatic: Successive sages polished codes.

sentences.zh: 自軍興以來，法度陵替，至於處事不用律令，競作屬命，人立異議，曲適物情，虧傷大例。

translations.literal: Since military emergencies regulations slipped until offices avoided statutes—every house issued commands, every voice differed—twisting sentiment wounded grand norms.
translations.idiomatic: Warlord adjudication shredded Jin law.

sentences.zh: 府立節度，復不奉用，臨事改制，朝作夕改，至於主者不敢任法，每輒關咨，委之大官，非為政之體。

translations.literal: Headquarters issue directives yet offices ignore them—changing rules morning and evening—clerks dare not apply law, always consulting superiors, abdicating to grandees—not governance style.
translations.idiomatic: Rotating edicts paralyzed local judges.

sentences.zh: 若本曹處事不合法令，監司當以法彈違，不得動用開塞，以壞成事。

translations.literal: If a bureau acts contrary to statute, inspectorates must impeach by law—may not open or block ad hoc to wreck finished cases.
translations.idiomatic: Censorates must guard statutory review.

sentences.zh: 按法蓋粗術，非妙道也，矯割物情，以成法耳。

translations.literal: Law is coarse craft, not subtle path—it trims sentiment to complete institutions.
translations.idiomatic: Law approximates justice mechanically.

sentences.zh: 若每隨物情，輒改法制，此為以情壞法。

translations.literal: If each time sentiment shifts statutes change, sentiment ruins law.
translations.idiomatic: Sentiment-driven amendment corrupts law.

sentences.zh: 法之不一，是謂多門，開人事之路，廣私請之端，非先王立法之本意也。

translations.literal: Law’s lack of unity means many gates—opening personal lobbying and widening private requests—not how former kings founded law.
translations.idiomatic: Multiple legal doors invite corruption.

sentences.zh: 凡為駁議者，若違律令節度，當合經傳及前比故事，不得任情以破成法。

translations.literal: All dissenters violating statute procedure must cite classics, precedents, and prior comparators—may not indulge emotion to break settled law.
translations.idiomatic: Appeals require textual authority.

sentences.zh: 愚謂宜令錄事更立條制，諸立議者皆當引律令經傳，不得直以情言，無所依准，以虧舊典也。

translations.literal: Your servant thinks recorders should draft standing rules: debaters must cite statutes and classics—never naked emotion lacking authority—to avoid harming old canons.
translations.idiomatic: Mandate citation standards for memorial debates.

sentences.zh: 若開塞隨宜，權道制物，此是人君之所得行，非臣子所宜專用。

translations.literal: If opening or blocking follows convenience—policy tricks manipulating facts—that is what lords may execute, not what subjects monopolize.
translations.idiomatic: Only sovereigns wield emergency discretion.

sentences.zh: 主者唯當徵文據法，以事為斷耳。」

translations.literal: Specialists must cite text and law, deciding by facts alone."
translations.idiomatic: Judges stick to facts under codified rules.

sentences.zh: 是時帝以權宜從事，尚未能從。

translations.literal: At the time the emperor followed expedients and could not yet adopt it.
translations.idiomatic: Exigent survival politics delayed reform.

sentences.zh: 而河東衛展為晉王大理，考擿故事有不合情者，又上書曰：「今施行詔書，有考子正父死刑，或鞭父母問子所在。

translations.literal: Hedong’s Wei Zhan, as Jin Prince’s director of great judgment, combed precedents for unreasonable points and memorialized: "Now applying edicts includes examining sons to fix fathers to capital death, or flogging parents to ask where sons are.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Zhan protested edicts torturing parents for children’s crimes.

sentences.zh: 近主者所稱《庚寅詔書》，舉家逃亡家長斬。

translations.literal: Recently handlers cite the Gengyin edict: whole households fleeing mean the household head is beheaded.
translations.idiomatic: The Gengyin order executed fugitive heads of household.

sentences.zh: 若長是逃亡之主，斬之雖重猶可。

translations.literal: If the elder truly leads the flight, beheading—though heavy—is tolerable.
translations.idiomatic: Decapitating actual fugitive elders seems harsh yet logical.

sentences.zh: 設子孫犯事，將考祖父逃亡，逃亡是子孫，而父祖嬰其酷。

translations.literal: Suppose grandchildren offend yet judges torture grandfathers about flights—the flight belongs to descendants yet ancestors suffer cruelty.
translations.idiomatic: Pinning flight guilt on grandparents when juniors fled reverses generations.

sentences.zh: 傷順破教，如此者眾。

translations.literal: Such cases wound compliance and break teaching—many exist.
translations.idiomatic: Many rulings violate moral order.

sentences.zh: 相隱之道離，則君臣之義廢。

translations.literal: When mutual concealment splits, lord-minister righteousness perishes.
translations.idiomatic: Destroying family silence erodes political loyalty.

sentences.zh: 君臣之義廢，則犯上之奸生矣。

translations.literal: When lord-minister righteousness perishes, crimes of betraying superiors arise.
translations.idiomatic: Broken loyalty breeds rebellion.

sentences.zh: 秦網密文峻，漢興，掃除煩苛，風移俗易，幾于刑厝。

translations.literal: Qin’s net was dense and writing harsh; Han arose sweeping bother—customs shifted until punishments nearly lay idle.
translations.idiomatic: Han softened Qin cruelty toward peace.

sentences.zh: 大人革命，不得不蕩其穢匿，通其圮滯。

translations.literal: Great men reforming destiny must scour filth and unblock stagnation.
translations.idiomatic: Founders purge prior abuses.

sentences.zh: 今詔書宜除者多，有便於當今，著為正條，則法差簡易。

translations.literal: Many edicts deserve repeal—whatever suits the present should become formal articles so law grows simpler.
translations.idiomatic: Codify useful waivers and discard cruel relics.

sentences.zh: 」元帝令曰：「禮樂不興，則刑罰不中，是以明罰敕法，先王所慎。

translations.literal: " Emperor Yuan replied: "When ritual and music fail to flourish punishments miss center—therefore clarifying punishments and correcting law former kings treated cautiously.
translations.idiomatic: Yuandi admits statutory chaos since Yuankang.

sentences.zh: 自元康已來，事故薦臻，法禁滋漫。

translations.literal: Since Yuankang years incidents multiplied endlessly; prohibitions swelled.
translations.idiomatic: Yuankang onward bred proliferating bans.

sentences.zh: 大理所上，宜朝堂會議，蠲除詔書不可用者，此孤所虛心者也。」

translations.literal: What the Minister of Justice submits should convene court conference to repeal unusable edicts—this orphan sincerely desires it."
translations.idiomatic: Yuandi orders court debate to purge bad edicts.

sentences.zh: 及帝即位，展為廷尉，又上言：「古者肉刑，事經前聖，漢文除之，增加大辟。

translations.literal: When the emperor ascended, Wei Zhan as commandant again stated: "Ancient corporal punishments passed sage validation; Emperor Wen removed them yet increased capital crimes.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Zhan renewed corporal debate from Ministry of Justice.

sentences.zh: 今人戶凋荒，百不遺一，而刑法峻重，非句踐養胎之義也。

translations.literal: Now households are devastated—not one in a hundred survives—yet punishments stay harsh—this is not Goujian’s nurture-the-womb kindness.
translations.idiomatic: Depopulation clashes with Goujian-style mercy.

sentences.zh: 愚謂宜復古施行，以隆太平之化。

translations.literal: Your servant thinks antiquity should return to practice to uplift great peace’s transformation.
translations.idiomatic: Wei urges restoring classical mutilation.

sentences.zh: 」詔內外通議。

translations.literal: " Edict ordered inner and outer courts deliberate.
translations.idiomatic: Court-wide deliberation ensued.

sentences.zh: 於是驃騎將軍王導、太常賀循、侍中紀瞻、中書郎庾亮、大將軍諮議參軍梅陶、散騎郎張嶷等議，以：「肉刑之典，由來尚矣。

translations.literal: Thereupon General Who Inspires Might Wang Dao, Minister of Ceremonies He Xun, Palace Attendant Ji Zhan, Secretariat Gentleman Yu Liang, staff adviser Mei Tao, Gentleman Zhang Ni and others argued that corporal statutes descend from deep antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao’s bloc defended classical mutilation.

sentences.zh: 肇自古先，以及三代，聖哲明王所未曾改也。

translations.literal: From earliest ancestors through three dynasties sagely enlightened kings never altered them.
translations.idiomatic: Three-age kings kept mutilation.

sentences.zh: 豈是漢文常主所能易者乎！

translations.literal: How could mere Emperor Wen of Han alter them!
translations.idiomatic: Han Wendi was no sage legislator.

sentences.zh: 時蕭曹已沒，絳灌之徒不能正其義。

translations.literal: At that time Xiao He and Cao Shen had died—subordinates like Zhou Bo could not straighten principle.
translations.idiomatic: Early Han lacked wise ministers to defend classical law.

sentences.zh: 逮班固深論其事，以為外有輕刑之名，內實殺人。

translations.literal: When Ban Gu examined deeply he judged outwardly lighter punishments inwardly killed more.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu exposed Wen’s reform as bloodier.

sentences.zh: 又死刑太重，生刑太輕，生刑縱於上，死刑怨於下，輕重失當，故刑政不中也。

translations.literal: Further capital death weighs too heavy while living punishments weigh too light—living lax above, capital bitter below—imbalance misorders punishments.
translations.idiomatic: Wen’s imbalance caused penal dysfunction.

sentences.zh: 且原先王之造刑也，非以過怒也，非以殘人也，所以救奸，所以當罪。

translations.literal: Moreover former kings crafting punishments acted not from excess anger nor desire to maim but to rescue society and match guilt.
translations.idiomatic: Classical mutilation targeted rehabilitation.

sentences.zh: 今盜者竊人之財，淫者好人之色，亡者避叛之役，皆無殺害也，則加之以刑。

translations.literal: Now thieves steal lust seduces fugitives flee corvée—none kills yet punishments apply.
translations.idiomatic: Non-capital crimes received death.

sentences.zh: 刑之則止，而加之斬戮，戮過其罪，死不可生，縱虐於此，歲以巨計。

translations.literal: Punishment should stop yet waist-cutting adds killing—execution exceeds guilt—death cannot revive—such cruelty yearly tallies vast.
translations.idiomatic: Death sentences overshot proportion annually.

sentences.zh: 此乃仁人君子所不忍聞，而況行之於政乎！

translations.literal: This benevolent gentlemen cannot bear hearing—how execute policy!
translations.idiomatic: Mass execution horrifies humane ears.

sentences.zh: 若乃惑其名而不練其實，惡其生而趣其死，此畏水投舟，避坎蹈井，愚夫之不若，何取於政哉！

translations.literal: If deluded by reputation ignoring substance hating life rushing death—that fears water yet boards boat avoids pit yet leaps well—fools exceed such conduct—what governance values that!
translations.idiomatic: Rejecting mutilation for killing is suicidal stupidity.

sentences.zh: 今大晉中興，遵復古典，率由舊章，起千載之滯義，拯百殘之遺黎，使皇典廢而復存，黔首死而更生，至義暢於三代之際，遺風播乎百世之後，生肉枯骨，惠侔造化，豈不休哉！

translations.literal: Now Great Jin restores antiquity following old chapters raising stalled righteousness rescuing maimed survivors reviving sagely canons raising dead commoners—supreme righteousness spanning three ages merit flowing hundred generations flesh growing on bones kindness rivaling creation—is this not splendid!
translations.idiomatic: Great Jin’s revival supposedly resurrected classical statutes and redeemed ruined peoples—your rhetoric celebrates restoring sagely standards and granting commoners new life as though Jin matched the virtue of the Three Ages and healed flesh onto bone; yet that lofty praise collapses if lighter punishments merely mutilate the law-abiding.

sentences.zh: 惑者乃曰，死猶不懲，而況于刑？

translations.literal: Critics say death still fails to deter—how much less mutilation?
translations.idiomatic: Skeptics ask whether mutilation deters.

sentences.zh: 然人者冥也，其至愚矣，雖加斬戮，忽為灰土，死事日往，生欲日存，未以為改。

translations.literal: Yet humans are benighted—most foolish—even executions vanish them to ash daily death dulls desire—few reform.
translations.idiomatic: Death’s abstraction fails deterrence.

sentences.zh: 若刑諸市朝，朝夕鑒戒，刑者詠為惡之永痛，惡者睹殘刖之長廢，故足懼也。

translations.literal: If executing in marketplace morning and evening offers mirror—criminals chant wicked pain forever villains glimpse lifelong maiming—then awe suffices.
